title: Docker — Images, Layers & Networking
summary: Docker images are not magic — they're stacked layers with a union filesystem on top. Understanding this model explains why your images are large, why build caching works (or doesn't), and what's actually happening when a container 'runs'.

sections.title: How image layers work
sections.body:
## What Are Image Layers?

A Docker image is not a single monolithic blob — it is a series of **read-only filesystem layers** stacked on top of each other using a union filesystem (OverlayFS on modern Linux). Each instruction in a Dockerfile that modifies the filesystem (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) produces a new layer. The final image is the union of all those layers presented as a single coherent filesystem to the container.

This design exists for two reasons: **deduplication** and **build caching**. If two images share the same base layer (e.g., `python:3.12-slim`), that layer is stored only once on disk and in a registry. When you push or pull an image, only the layers that differ need to transfer — which dramatically reduces bandwidth and storage costs in real CI/CD pipelines.

At runtime, Docker adds a thin **writable container layer** on top of the read-only image layers. This is where all file modifications, log writes, and temporary data live during a container's lifetime. When the container is removed, this writable layer is discarded — which is why containers are considered ephemeral.

**Why build cache invalidation matters in practice:** If you place an instruction that changes frequently (e.g., `COPY . .`) before a slow instruction (e.g., `RUN pip install`), every code change forces `pip install` to re-run from scratch. In a team running hundreds of CI builds per day, this adds up to hours of wasted compute. Understanding layer ordering is one of the highest-leverage Dockerfile optimizations available.

**The model:** a Docker image is a stack of read-only layers. Each `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD` instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer. The container adds a thin writable layer on top at runtime.

```
[ writable container layer ]   ← only this layer changes at runtime
─────────────────────────────
[ COPY ./app /app ]            ← layer 4
[ RUN pip install -r req.txt ] ← layer 3
[ COPY requirements.txt . ]    ← layer 2
[ FROM python:3.12-slim ]      ← layer 1 (base image, itself many layers)
```

**Why this matters for caching:**
- Docker caches layers. If a layer hasn't changed, it uses the cache.
- Cache is **invalidated for all layers after** the changed one.
- Order your Dockerfile from least-changing to most-changing.

```dockerfile
# BAD order — changes to app code invalidate pip install cache
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY . .                    # changes every time → invalidates next layer
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # always re-runs

# GOOD order — copy requirements first, copy code second
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY requirements.txt .     # only changes when deps change
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # cached until deps change
COPY . .                    # changes often, but only affects this layer
```

**Layer inspection:**

```bash norun
# See image layers and sizes
docker image history my-app:latest

# See layer details
docker inspect my-app:latest | jq '.[0].RootFS.Layers'

# What's actually in each layer (dive tool is great for this)
dive my-app:latest
```

sections.title: Writing production Dockerfiles
sections.body:
## Writing Production-Ready Dockerfiles

Most developers start with a Dockerfile that works and stop there. A production Dockerfile has additional requirements: **minimal image size** (smaller attack surface, faster pulls), **build reproducibility** (pinned versions, no floating tags), **security** (non-root user, no unnecessary packages), and **build efficiency** (cache-friendly layer ordering).

The single most impactful pattern is the **multi-stage build**. Before multi-stage builds existed, teams would either ship bloated images containing compilers and build tools, or maintain complex wrapper scripts to build artifacts outside Docker and copy them in. Multi-stage builds solve this natively: you use one stage with full build tooling to produce artifacts, and a second minimal stage that copies only those artifacts. The final image has no compiler, no build dependencies, no source code — just the runtime and your compiled output.

**Security considerations that belong in every production Dockerfile:**

| Practice | Why It Matters |
|---|---|
| Pin base image to a digest or exact tag | Prevents silent upstream changes that introduce vulnerabilities |
| Run as a non-root user | Limits blast radius if the app is compromised |
| Use `--no-install-recommends` for apt | Avoids pulling in packages you never use |
| Clean package manager caches in the same `RUN` step | Prevents cache files from inflating the layer size |
| Use `.dockerignore` | Prevents secrets and large files from entering the build context |

A poorly ordered Dockerfile can make a team's CI pipeline 3–5x slower than necessary. The best order is: things that change least often at the top, things that change most often at the bottom.

```dockerfile
# ── Multi-stage build — the most important pattern ────────
# Stage 1: build (has build tools, generates artifacts)
FROM python:3.12 AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
COPY src/ ./src/
RUN python -m compileall src/

# Stage 2: runtime (minimal — only what's needed to run)
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
# Copy only the installed packages and compiled code
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY --from=builder /build/src ./src/
COPY entrypoint.sh .

ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# Don't run as root
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash appuser
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "-m", "uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]

# ── Best practices ─────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. Pin base image versions (never 'latest')
FROM python:3.12.3-slim-bookworm

# 2. Combine RUN commands to reduce layers
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# NOT:
# RUN apt-get update
# RUN apt-get install curl
# RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*   ← doesn't actually reduce image size

# 3. Use .dockerignore
# .dockerignore:
# .git
# .venv
# __pycache__
# *.pyc
# .env
# tests/
# *.md

# 4. COPY specific files, not entire directories
COPY requirements.txt pyproject.toml ./
# NOT: COPY . .

# 5. Use HEALTHCHECK
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
```

sections.title: Container networking
sections.body:
## How Container Networking Works

Every container gets its own **network namespace** — an isolated view of the Linux networking stack with its own IP address, routing table, and set of network interfaces. This is what makes `localhost` inside a container refer to the container itself, not the host machine. It is a frequent source of confusion when developers first start containerizing applications that previously ran directly on the host.

Docker implements networking through **drivers** that control how network namespaces are connected to each other and to the outside world. The default `bridge` driver creates a virtual network interface (`docker0`) on the host, assigns containers IP addresses in a private subnet (typically `172.17.0.0/16`), and sets up NAT rules so container traffic can reach the internet. Port publishing (`-p host:container`) creates additional NAT rules to forward traffic from the host port into the container.

**The critical practical detail** is the difference between the default bridge network and a **user-defined bridge network**. On the default bridge, containers can communicate by IP address but not by name. On a user-defined bridge, Docker provides automatic DNS resolution so containers can reach each other using their `--name` as a hostname. This is why Docker Compose-based services can reference each other by service name — Compose creates a user-defined bridge network automatically.

In a microservices architecture, network design is a security control. Databases should only be reachable by the services that need them, not exposed to all containers. Docker Compose lets you define multiple networks and control which services join which — effectively implementing network segmentation without additional infrastructure.

**Why it matters:** understanding Docker networking explains why `localhost` inside a container doesn't mean the same as `localhost` on your host, and why containers can talk to each other by name.

```
Host machine (172.17.0.1)
  └── docker0 bridge network
        ├── container-a (172.17.0.2)
        └── container-b (172.17.0.3)
```

**The four network drivers:**

- **bridge** (default): containers get their own IP, isolated from host. Containers on the same bridge can communicate.
- **host**: container shares host's network stack. No isolation, but no overhead. Useful for performance-sensitive workloads.
- **none**: no networking. Useful for batch jobs that don't need the network.
- **overlay**: spans multiple Docker hosts. Used by Docker Swarm.

```bash norun
# User-defined bridge networks are better than default
# (containers can reach each other by NAME)
docker network create my-app-network

docker run -d --name postgres \
    --network my-app-network \
    postgres:16

docker run -d --name my-app \
    --network my-app-network \
    -e DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:5432/mydb \
    my-app:latest
# my-app can connect to 'postgres:5432' — name resolution works!

# Docker Compose handles this automatically
# All services in a compose file are on the same network by default

# Port mapping: -p host:container
docker run -p 8080:80 nginx   # host:8080 → container:80

# Inspect networking
docker network ls
docker network inspect my-app-network
docker inspect my-app | jq '.[0].NetworkSettings.Networks'
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml — networks
services:
  backend:
    networks:
      - internal
      - external

  database:
    networks:
      - internal   # only reachable by backend, not exposed

  nginx:
    networks:
      - external
    ports:
      - "80:80"

networks:
  internal:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true  # no external internet access
  external:
    driver: bridge
```

sections.title: Volumes and persistence
sections.body:
## Data Persistence in Docker

Containers are **stateless by design**. The writable container layer that sits on top of the image layers is tied to the lifetime of that specific container instance — when you run `docker rm`, it is gone. This is intentional: stateless containers are easier to scale horizontally, replace on failure, and upgrade by swapping images. But real applications have state: databases, uploaded files, configuration generated at runtime, audit logs.

Docker provides three mechanisms for persisting data beyond a container's lifetime:

| Mechanism | Managed by | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Named volumes** | Docker | Databases, persistent app data — Docker manages the storage location |
| **Bind mounts** | You | Development (live code reloading), injecting config files from the host |
| **Anonymous volumes** | Docker | Rarely: one-off scratch space with no need for future access |

**Named volumes are the recommended default for production data.** Docker stores them under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/` and gives them stable identifiers. They survive `docker rm`, they can be backed up with `docker run --rm -v vol:/data alpine tar`, and they work correctly across container restarts and upgrades.

**Bind mounts are ideal for development** — mounting your local source directory into the container lets you edit code with your host editor and see changes immediately without rebuilding the image. Avoid bind mounts in production for application data, as they create tight coupling between the container and the host's filesystem layout.

**Anonymous volumes are a footgun.** If you write `volumes: - /some/path` in Compose (without a named volume reference), Docker creates a new anonymous volume on every `docker compose up`. Your data appears to persist within a session but vanishes when you run `docker compose down -v` or when the volume is garbage-collected. Always use named volumes for anything you care about.

**The core rule:** containers are ephemeral. Anything written to the container filesystem is lost when the container is removed. Volumes are for data that must survive.

```bash norun
# Named volumes — managed by Docker, persist between container restarts
docker volume create postgres-data
docker run -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

# Bind mounts — mount a host path into the container
docker run -v /host/path:/container/path my-app
docker run -v $(pwd)/config:/app/config:ro my-app  # :ro = read-only

# Anonymous volumes — not recommended (no stable name)
docker run -v /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

# The bug from your OCH-2468 investigation:
# 'volumes: - /path' in compose creates an ANONYMOUS volume
# Each container start gets a NEW anonymous volume → data lost!

# Fix: use a NAMED volume
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  orchestra:
    image: orchestra:latest
    volumes:
      # BAD (anonymous):
      # - /opt/orchestra/security
      # GOOD (named):
      - orchestra-security:/opt/orchestra/security

volumes:
  orchestra-security:   # defined here → named, persists
```

```bash norun
# Inspect volumes
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect postgres-data

# Backup a volume
docker run --rm \
    -v postgres-data:/data \
    -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/postgres-backup.tar.gz -C /data .

# Restore
docker run --rm \
    -v postgres-data:/data \
    -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar xzf /backup/postgres-backup.tar.gz -C /data
```

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.body:
## Docker CLI Reference

After working through the concepts of layers, Dockerfiles, networking, and volumes, you need to be fluent with the Docker CLI to put them into practice. The commands below cover the full lifecycle: building images, running and managing containers, handling volumes, and inspecting networks.

A few patterns worth internalizing:

- **`docker run --rm`** is your best friend for one-off tasks — the container cleans itself up automatically.
- **`docker exec -it <container> bash`** lets you get a shell inside a running container for live debugging without stopping it.
- **`docker logs -f`** streams logs in real time, equivalent to `tail -f` for container output.
- **`docker image prune` and `docker system prune`** reclaim disk space eaten by dangling images and stopped containers — critical on CI runners and development machines that build frequently.
- Dockerfile instructions like `EXPOSE` and `LABEL` are documentation for humans and tooling — they do not enforce anything. `EXPOSE` does not publish a port; you still need `-p` in `docker run`.

The `exec` form of `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` (`["executable", "arg"]`) is preferred over the shell form (`executable arg`) because it does not wrap the process in a shell — signals like `SIGTERM` reach your process directly, which matters for graceful shutdown.

```bash norun
# ── Images ────────────────────────────────────────
docker build -t name:tag .        # build
docker build -t name:tag -f path/Dockerfile .  # custom Dockerfile
docker image ls                   # list images
docker image rm name:tag          # remove
docker image history name:tag     # show layers
docker image prune                # remove dangling images

# ── Containers ────────────────────────────────────
docker run -d --name ctr image    # detached
docker run -it image bash         # interactive
docker run --rm image             # auto-remove on exit
docker run -p 8080:80 image       # port mapping
docker run -e KEY=val image       # env var
docker run -v vol:/path image     # volume

docker ps                         # running containers
docker ps -a                      # all containers
docker logs ctr                   # view logs
docker logs -f ctr                # follow logs
docker exec -it ctr bash          # shell into running container
docker stop ctr && docker rm ctr  # stop + remove

# ── Volumes ───────────────────────────────────────
docker volume ls
docker volume create my-vol
docker volume rm my-vol
docker volume prune

# ── Networks ──────────────────────────────────────
docker network ls
docker network create my-net
docker network connect my-net ctr
docker network inspect my-net

# ── Dockerfile key instructions ──────────────────
FROM image:tag          # base image (always pin)
RUN cmd                 # execute during build
COPY src dst            # copy files (prefer over ADD)
ADD src dst             # like COPY + auto-extract archives
ENV KEY=val             # env var available at runtime
ARG KEY=val             # build-time variable
WORKDIR /path           # set working directory
EXPOSE port             # document the port (not publish)
USER username           # run as non-root
CMD ["exec", "form"]    # default command
ENTRYPOINT ["exec"]    # fixed entrypoint
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD curl -f http://localhost/health
```

sections.title: Quiz
sections.body:
## Applying What You've Learned

The questions below test the mental models that make Docker usage reliable in practice — not just trivia, but the thinking patterns that prevent real production incidents. Common Docker mistakes that make it into production include: images built with a `COPY . .` early in the Dockerfile (destroying cache efficiency), databases using anonymous volumes (losing data on every `docker compose down`), containers run as root (widening blast radius on compromise), and services bound together on the default bridge network (no name-based resolution, surprising connectivity failures).

Before running the exercise commands at the bottom: you are already inside a Docker container running on a real k3s cluster. The Python environment, tools like `kubectl` and `aws`, and the directory structure of the backend are all Docker constructs. Examining what's installed, how the environment is configured, and what the container's OS looks like is itself a form of Docker introspection — everything you observe is the result of a Dockerfile and a `docker compose` definition.

The scaffolded Dockerfile at the end is intentionally incomplete. Filling it in requires applying layer-ordering discipline, selecting the right base image, and thinking about what should and should not be included in a production image.

**Q1.** You change a line in your application code. In a well-structured Dockerfile, which layers are rebuilt?

**Q2.** What's the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`?

**Q3.** A container writes data to `/data/output.txt`. You stop and remove the container. Is the file still accessible? How would you fix it?

**Q4.** Two containers need to communicate by hostname. What network configuration do you need?

---

**Answers:**

**A1.** Only the layer that copies the application code and all subsequent layers. If `requirements.txt` didn't change, the `pip install` layer is served from cache (this is why copy-requirements-then-code order matters).

**A2.** `CMD` is the default command — it can be overridden by arguments to `docker run`. `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed executable — arguments to `docker run` are passed as arguments to it. Use `ENTRYPOINT` for the binary, `CMD` for default arguments: `ENTRYPOINT ["python3"]` + `CMD ["-m", "uvicorn", "main:app"]`.

**A3.** The file is lost — container filesystems are ephemeral. Fix: mount a named volume at `/data` so the output persists beyond the container's lifetime.

**A4.** Both containers need to be on the same user-defined bridge network. Docker then provides DNS resolution so containers can reach each other by their `--name`.

---

**Exercise:**

```bash
# Explore the learning app's own container from inside the terminal
# (you're already inside a Docker container!)
cat /etc/os-release
which python3 && python3 --version
pip list | grep -E 'boto3|kubernetes|requests|click'
ls /usr/local/bin/
env | grep -E 'AWS|KUBE|PATH' | sort

# Write a minimal Dockerfile for a Python DevOps script
cat > /tmp/Dockerfile << 'EOF'
FROM python:3.12-slim

# TODO: add a non-root user
# TODO: install jq and curl
# TODO: copy and install requirements
# TODO: copy the script
# TODO: set the entrypoint
EOF
cat /tmp/Dockerfile
```
